To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Middle–Late Oxfordian interval was characterized by the predominance of oxic conditions, whereas the Upper Bajocalvian through the Lower Callovian interval was characterized predominately by the occurrence of dysoxic conditions, which is in agreement with the global climate conditions of the Middle–Late Jurasssic.
the redox conditions in Middle–Late Jurassic pelagic sediments from the Alpine Tethyan domain changed significantly, with the highest oxygen levels recorded in the Upper Oxfordian.

(1) the Middle–Late Oxfordian was a time of major changes in redox conditions in pelagic sediments in the Alpine Tethyan realm; (2) this change is related to the long-term variations in atmospheric circulation, which were driven by the sea surface temperature contrast between the equatorial and subtropical regions of the Tethys; and (3) this change is linked to global warming, as indicated by a decrease in the strength of the mean equatorial atmospheric circulation.

the long-term trend of the redox potential is controlled by the global climate change.

the Middle–Late Oxfordian period was a transitional stage between the long-term periods of the Middle Jurassic and the Early Late Jurassic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the redox potential (as well as other redox proxies) can be used to reconstruct changes in the climate of the Jurassic Tethys.
the redox state of the Tethys pelagic environment changed in response to the changes in SST and the intensity of the atmospheric circulation, which were driven by the global climate change.
